name: Deutsche Umwelthilfe v Freistaat Bayern (C-752/18) – enforcement of the Munich air quality plan judgment
date: 9 October 2012 (Verwaltungsgericht München, judgment); 21 June 2016 and 27 February 2017 (threats of penalty payments); 26 October 2017 and 28 January 2018 (penalty payments imposed); 9 November 2018 (reference to the CJEU by the Bayerischer Verwaltungsgerichtshof); 19 December 2019 (CJEU, Grand Chamber)

jurisdiction.court: Verwaltungsgericht München (Munich Administrative Court); Bayerischer Verwaltungsgerichtshof (Higher Administrative Court of Bavaria); Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) – Grand Chamber (preliminary ruling)

description: By a final judgment of 9 October 2012, delivered in an action brought by the environmental association Deutsche Umwelthilfe, the Verwaltungsgericht München ordered the Land of Bavaria to amend the air quality plan for Munich so as to include the measures necessary to comply as soon as possible with the annual NO2 limit value, which was exceeded, sometimes very considerably, on several kilometres of road in the city. As the Land did not comply, the courts threatened and then imposed penalty payments (EUR 10,000 threatened in 2016; EUR 2,000 to 4,000 threatened by the Bayerischer Verwaltungsgerichtshof on 27 February 2017, including for the failure to provide for traffic bans on certain diesel vehicles; EUR 4,000 imposed on 26 October 2017 and again on 28 January 2018). Representatives of the Land, including its Minister-President, publicly stated that they would not comply. The Verwaltungsgericht dismissed Deutsche Umwelthilfe’s application for the coercive detention of the Bavarian Minister for the Environment or of the Minister-President; on appeal, the Bayerischer Verwaltungsgerichtshof asked the CJEU whether EU law requires or authorises such detention, since penalty payments paid by the Land into its own budget had no deterrent effect.
outcome: The CJEU (Grand Chamber) held that, where a national authority persistently refuses to comply with a judicial decision enjoining it to perform a clear, precise and unconditional obligation flowing from EU law, in particular from Directive 2008/50/EC, the national court must order the coercive detention of office holders involved in the exercise of official authority where domestic law contains a legal basis for such detention which is sufficiently accessible, precise and foreseeable in its application, and provided that the resulting limitation of the right to liberty (Article 6 of the Charter) complies with Article 52(1) of the Charter. If there is no such legal basis in domestic law, EU law does not empower the court to have recourse to such a measure. The judgment rests on the right to an effective remedy (first paragraph of Article 47 of the Charter).
